summary: Hostnames, URIs, IP addresses, and email addresses are often compared when making security decisions. If different parties use different comparison algorithms, the result can be a security hole. This informational document discusses these identifier comparison issues.

plainLanguage.summary: Security systems often compare names before granting access. This RFC explains how different comparison rules can let an attacker through or block a legitimate user.

questions: why comparing hostnames and uris is risky
why is identifier comparison a security risk
what is a false positive in identifier comparison
what are absolute definite and indefinite identifiers
what is a false positive in identifier matching
subtitle: Security risks when different systems compare the same identifier in different ways

tldr.problem: Systems use hostnames, URIs, addresses and email identifiers to make security decisions. If two parties compare the same identifier differently, they may grant access to the wrong party or deny legitimate access.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC classifies identifiers as Absolute, Definite or Indefinite, explains false positives and negatives, and surveys comparison problems in common identifier types.
tldr.outcome: It recommends specifying a stable comparison algorithm for new identifiers and examining differences when multiple protocols use the same identifier.

today: RFC 6943 is an Informational document from the Internet Architecture Board, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides discussion and design guidance, not a comparison protocol.

sections.title: Identifiers and Comparison
sections.content:
Identifiers are generated, distributed and later supplied to a repository or service for matching. The form may change between these steps: an identifier can be printed, spoken, embedded in another identifier or transmitted electronically. This document concerns whether two identifiers are the same identifier, not whether two different identifiers refer to the same entity.

The RFC distinguishes Absolute identifiers, compared byte by byte; Definite identifiers, with one well-defined comparison algorithm; and Indefinite identifiers, for which there is no single comparison method. Canonicalization converts an identifier to a standard form before comparison, so every participant needs to use the same form and algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Two systems need the same rules to decide whether two names match. Some names have one clear comparison rule, while others depend on context or convention.

sections.title: False Matches and Security Decisions
sections.content:
A false positive occurs when two different identifiers compare as equal. A false negative occurs when two identifiers for the same thing compare as different. Their effect depends on the policy: with “grant on match,” a false positive can elevate privilege and a false negative can deny service; with “deny on match,” the effects reverse.

The RFC gives a hypothetical account example where one party includes a URI fragment in comparisons and another ignores it. An attacker registers an account containing a fragment and then uses a token for that account to request the unfragmented resource. Because the parties compare the URI differently, the resource holder accepts the token for the wrong account.
sections.plainLanguage: If one system treats two different names as equal, it may grant access to the wrong person. If systems treat the same name as different, they may block a legitimate request.

sections.title: Hostnames, Addresses, URIs and Email
sections.content:
“Hostname” can mean an entire domain name or only one label, so specifications need to define it. IPv4 strings can use loose or strict forms, and a short string may be ambiguous between an address and a hostname. IPv6 addresses also have multiple equivalent text forms, so comparing binary addresses avoids some string-format differences.

URI comparison depends on the scheme and on choices about user information, paths, queries and fragments. Email-address-like identifiers are also difficult because each domain defines its own local-part rules. Resolving two hostnames to IP addresses to compare them is unreliable because addresses can be dynamic, private or location-dependent, and the lookup can reveal information about a security decision.
sections.plainLanguage: The same address can have several text forms, and some strings can be interpreted as either a hostname or an IP address. URI parts and email usernames also need clear comparison rules.

sections.title: Internationalization, Scope and Time
sections.content:
Internationalized identifiers can be represented using different encodings, and characters can look or sound alike without being identical. A comparison system should validate the identifier after or as part of canonicalization, so encoded delimiters cannot change how the identifier is parsed. Case-insensitive comparisons also need a defined rule because character mappings can depend on locale.

Identifiers may only be unique within a particular scope, such as a host or organization. They may also be reassigned later. If access-control lists or cached lookup results are not updated when the identifier changes owner, a system may apply old permissions to a new entity.
sections.plainLanguage: Names may look alike, depend on local context or be reassigned later. Systems need to validate names consistently and update stored permissions when an identifier's owner or scope changes.

sections.title: Recommendations for Identifier Designers
sections.content:
A system that needs both allow and deny decisions within the same identifier space should avoid Indefinite identifiers for security comparisons. New identifiers should specify an Absolute or Definite comparison algorithm, including how ambiguity and future extensions are handled.

When an architecture combines several protocols, designers should compare the algorithms each protocol uses for the same identifier. The RFC identifies this as a difficult issue and leaves solutions for current systems as future work.
sections.plainLanguage: When defining a new identifier, specify exactly how systems compare it. When several protocols share identifiers, check that they use compatible rules.
